note: Builds on 1.3 (atomic number, mass number, nuclear notation). Sets up 1.5 without teaching weighted average. 50-minute period; last 5 minutes are cleanup/reset.

fields.headline:
1.4
Isotopes
fields.subhead: Count protons, neutrons, and electrons in any isotope, and explain why the neutron count does not change the element.

fields.headline: Same Element, Different Mass
fields.subhead: Two atoms of carbon can have different masses. They are still both carbon.
fields.c1_b:
Protons.
Every carbon atom has 6.

Change that and you no longer have carbon.
fields.c2_b:
Neutrons.
Carbon can have 6, 7, or 8.

The mass changes. The element does not.
fields.mustwrite: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.

fields.headline: What Actually Names an Atom
fields.subhead: You already know the atomic number identifies the element. This section is what happens when the neutron count changes and the atomic number does not.
fields.keyq: If two atoms have different masses, how do you know they are the same element?

fields.headline: The Three Isotopes of Hydrogen
fields.subhead: Hydrogen is the clearest case: one proton in all three, and the neutron count does the rest.
fields.k1_b:
1 proton
0 neutrons
Mass number 1

About 99.98% of all hydrogen.
fields.k2_b:
1 proton
1 neutron
Mass number 2

Called deuterium.
fields.k3_b:
1 proton
2 neutrons
Mass number 3

Called tritium. Radioactive.
fields.mustwrite: The atomic number identifies the element. The mass number does not.

fields.headline: Two Ways to Write the Same Isotope
fields.subhead: You will see both. They carry exactly the same information.
fields.diagram:
Nuclear symbol and hyphen notation
for carbon-14, side by side
fields.a1_b: carbon-14. Element name, then mass number.
fields.a2_b: Mass number on top, atomic number below, element symbol beside.
fields.a3_b: Neither one shows you the neutrons. You calculate those.

fields.headline: Getting Neutrons Out of the Notation
fields.subhead: Four steps, and you use the same four every time.
fields.s1_b: Find the atomic number on the periodic table. That is your protons.
fields.s2_b: Read it from the notation. It is protons plus neutrons.
fields.s3_b: Neutrons = mass number minus atomic number.
fields.s4_b: Neutral atom only: electrons equal protons.

fields.headline: Example: Counting Particles in Chlorine-37
fields.subhead: Work area stays empty. We do this one together on the board.
fields.problem: How many protons, neutrons, and electrons are in a neutral atom of chlorine-37?
fields.mustwrite: Neutrons = mass number minus atomic number.

fields.headline: Chlorine-37, Worked
fields.subhead: Write the subtraction down. If you do it in your head you will lose track of it on the test.
fields.mustwrite: A neutral atom has equal protons and electrons. Chlorine-35 would give 18 neutrons.

fields.headline: Not All Isotopes Are Equally Common
fields.subhead: Isotopes of an element occur in fixed proportions. Those proportions are measured, not chosen.
fields.c1_b:
About 76% of all chlorine on Earth.

18 neutrons.
fields.mustwrite: Natural abundance is why the periodic table lists 35.45 and not a whole number.

fields.headline: Your Turn: Potassium-40
fields.subhead: Same four steps. Work it in your notes, then we compare.
fields.problem: How many protons, neutrons, and electrons are in a neutral atom of potassium-40?
fields.g1_b:
Potassium-40
Use the periodic table for the atomic number.
fields.mustwrite: Check your answer: does protons plus neutrons give you back the mass number?
